policies.none: no cache: recompute at every lookup
policies.repo: whole repository: any changed file (git blob) anywhere invalidates every entry
policies.file: file level: invalidate when a file of the dependency set (files of every node and edge read, evidence paths and both endpoints' paths) has a different git blob id
policies.fact_pos: EXTRA ROW, not in the brief: fact level on recorded positive facts only (whole-record hashes), no negative dependencies
policies.fact: fact level: invalidate when a recorded node or edge record (whole-record hash, line numbers and token counts included) changed or vanished, or a recorded query pattern's matched set changed (negative dependency)
policies.fact_sem: EXTRA ROW, not in the brief: as fact, but a fact read without its line or token fields is compared on a hash of its semantic fields only
policies.cutoff: fact level with early cutoff: on a changed dependency of a sub-derivation (a reach set, the ranked file list) the sub-derivation is recomputed and, if its result is equal, the answer that rests on it is kept without re-deriving
policies.cutoff_sem: EXTRA ROW: early cutoff on the semantic hashes of fact_sem
policies.ttl5: time to live: served while the answer is at most 5 first-parent commits old, no dependency tracking
policies.never: no invalidation at all (the stale control)

token_estimate.correction: An earlier version labelled the median-price column an upper bound ("at most about 58,100 tokens per 100 lookups"). A median is not a maximum: the audit (AUDIT.md section 7) gives 161,515 at mean prices and 185,388 at per-kind prices for fact.
token_estimate.completion: The completion kind has no measured derivation price and is left out.

what_it_shows: On this repository's history (190 parser-built snapshots, 2026-05-31 to 2026-08-03, 189 replay steps, 159 of them one commit apart) and on 250 structured questions of 8 kinds, a fact-level dependency record with negative dependencies served 25,490 of 29,097 lookups (87.6 %) from the cache and served 0 stale answers; with the semantic-field variant 27,896 (95.9 %) and with early cutoff on it 27,982 (96.2 %), also 0 stale. 'Stale' is judged against the same extractor's facts, not against the code. On the 112 questions whose answer changes at least once (15,240 lookups) the rates are 82.5 % (fact), 93.8 % (fact_sem) and 94.2 % (cutoff_sem), with 0 stale. An independent recomputation of all 40,880 warm tree-lane lookups agreed at every lookup (AUDIT.md).

Zero stale answers in 25,490 served answers gives a one-sided 95 % upper bound of about 0.012 % per served answer if lookups were independent; they are not (the same 250 questions repeat over 190 snapshots), and counted per question (0 of 250 questions ever served a stale answer) the bound is 1.19 % of questions.

File-level invalidation served 25,162 lookups (86.5 %) but 1,632 of them were stale (6.5 % of served answers, upper 95 % bound 6.75 %); 69 of the 250 questions served at least one stale answer. On the 112 changing questions it served 80.9 % with 13.2 % of served answers stale. Almost all of these come from negative dependencies: a new caller, test, invariant, migration or setting reader appearing in a file outside the answer's own files.

Dependency cases (an answer changed between consecutive lookups although none of its own files changed): 150 in 44 of the 189 steps, 134 of them in kinds 1-8 and 16 in the completion kind. In kinds 1-8, 133 of the 134 were a query pattern gaining or losing a match (negative dependency) and 1 was a recorded fact changing while its file did not (a route id whose prefix is set in another file). In the completion kind 11 were co-change edges recomputed from git history (no file content changed) and 5 were new edges.

Fact level without negative dependencies (extra row fact_pos) served 1,750 stale answers (6.8 % of served), as many as the file level: tracking which recorded facts changed does not protect an answer that says 'nothing else'; the query pattern has to be recorded too.

Fact level with whole-record hashes recomputes often for nothing: 3,203 of its 3,607 recomputations (88.8 %) returned the same answer, mostly because line numbers and token counts in node and edge records shift when unrelated lines of the same file move. Comparing only the fields the program read (fact_sem) cut recomputations to 1,201 (797 avoidable) with no stale answer.

Time-to-live policies trade hits for stale answers with no way to tell which is which: 5 commits served 79.6 % with 949 stale (4.1 % of served), 20 commits 94.4 % with 3,297 stale (12.0 %). No invalidation served everything and 9,520 answers (32.7 % of served) were stale; for answers cached 51 or more commits earlier 48.7 % of served answers were stale.

The completion ranking (unbounded reach, degree-normalised, top items inside 8,000 tokens) rests on a large part of the connected graph: a median of 3,633 nodes, 8,319 edges, 3,167 patterns and 323 files per answer (over every fresh answer at every snapshot), about 180 to 270 KB of dependency index per answer. Its answer changed in 2,802 of 11,783 consecutive steps (23.8 %), fact-level served only 9.2 % of lookups, early cutoff 24.5 %, and time-to-live 20 commits served 94.5 % with 64.8 % of them stale.

The hit rate falls as the gap between snapshots grows: on main's first-parent chain, every snapshot (mean gap 1.57 commits), every 2nd (3.14), 4th (6.33) and 8th (12.67) gave fact-level hit rates of 85.9, 76.7, 63.4 and 46.5 % and semantic-field hit rates of 94.9, 91.1, 84.4 and 73.8 %, still with 0 stale; file level's stale share of served answers rose from 5.8 to 9.2 %.
Whole-repository invalidation never served an answer: every one of the 189 steps changed at least one file.

Restricted to lookups whose fresh answer is not empty (20,349 of 29,097 in kinds 1-8), fact level served 85.1 %, the semantic variant 94.9 %, early cutoff on it 95.3 %, all with 0 stale; file level served 83.5 % with 9.6 % of them stale.

As an estimate under one assumption, not a bound and not a saving: if each served answer replaced one scripted-search derivation, fact level would avoid about 58,100 tokens per 100 lookups of kinds 1-8 at the finished test's median prices (694.5 tokens read, 31 tokens of answer), about 161,500 at its mean prices and about 185,400 at its per-kind median prices; against typed queries it avoids 0 tokens.

138 of the 250 questions of kinds 1-8 (55.2 %) never change their answer over the replay, and 13,857 of the 29,097 lookups (47.6 %) are of those questions; every policy is right on them, so rates over all questions are higher than on the questions that test invalidation.
what_it_does_not_show: It does not show that caching cuts an agent's tokens, turns or mistakes: no model and no agent ran, and every answer here is deterministic and cheap to recompute (247 questions in about 6 ms; a typed query returns each at about 31 tokens).
It does not test cached conclusions that cost a model many tokens to derive, which is the only case where the token bound could matter; nor how a model would use or misuse a cached answer.

It does not show how an agent would look things up: the replay scheduled every lookup itself (every live question at every snapshot). No agent decided whether or when to look something up, what to ask, or whether to trust a served answer.

It does not show that fact-level invalidation is safe in general: zero stale answers is what a correct recorder must give when a deterministic program reads the graph only through it, so it is expected by construction. It shows that this recorder has no gaps for these nine programs on this history; it does not carry over to conclusions a model draws from reads nobody records.

It does not show that fact-level invalidation is correct with respect to the code: the ground truth is the same extractor's facts recomputed at each snapshot, so an extraction error that persists is invisible here (design-check P15).

It does not show that the fact-level dependency recording is complete for other programs: the recording was designed with negative patterns from the start, and zero stale answers holds for these nine programs on this history only.

It does not test a temporal knowledge graph, validity intervals, model-extracted facts, documents read by a model, or graph type: the facts are the finished test's parser-built snapshots and the store is an in-memory graph.
It does not test traversal caching inside a single query, uncommitted working-tree edits, or caching within one agent session; snapshots are commits, mostly one commit apart.

It does not give a workload-weighted hit rate: every live question is looked up at every snapshot, which is not how sessions ask questions; 30 % of the kinds 1-8 lookups have an empty answer (63 % for change_reach, 60 % for screen_tables).

The token figure is an estimate, not a bound and not a saving: it assumes each served answer would otherwise cost one scripted-search derivation, its prices were measured once on 30 held-out questions (3 to 4 per kind) at one commit, the three ways of pricing differ by a factor of about 3, and it ignores the prompt-cache share and every other token bucket of a session.
The 'by age' hit rates are conditional on an answer having survived that long under each policy (a survival selection), not a decay curve of one answer.
It says nothing about other repositories, larger graphs, or change rates other than this repository's (about 155 first-parent commits on main over 9 weeks).

It does not give rates on a mix of changing questions: 55.2 % of the questions of kinds 1-8 never change and 47.6 % of the lookups are of those questions (rates on the changing questions are in results.static_and_changing_questions_tree).
It does not vary the anchor rule: questions were drawn only from anchors that live in at least 20 consecutive main-chain snapshots.
must_not_claim: Caching with invalidation saves tokens, or caching does not help (no tokens of any agent or model were measured; the answers cost almost nothing to recompute).

Fact-level invalidation is proven safe, or never serves a stale answer (zero stale is against the extractor's own facts, for nine fixed programs, on one history, and is expected by construction when every read is recorded).

The cache saves, or avoids at most, about 58,000 tokens per 100 lookups, or any stated token saving (the figure is an estimate at median prices, not a bound: mean prices give 161,515 and per-kind prices 185,388; nothing was measured; against typed queries it is 0).
Typed queries plus a cache answer questions 20 times cheaper, or 31 against 695 tokens is a session saving.
Early cutoff makes cached model conclusions cheap to keep fresh (only deterministic answers were tested).
A graph database, knowledge graph or temporal knowledge graph was tested here.
File-level caching serves 6.5 % stale answers in general, or is unsafe in general (13.2 % on the changing questions here; it depends on the question mix).

The hit rate an agent would see is 87.6 % or 95.9 % (the replay imposed the lookup schedule, 47.6 % of lookups are of questions that never change, and the empty-answer share and the gap between lookups both move it).
Hub questions cannot be cached (the completion kind was cached poorly because it rests on the whole graph; a smaller-budget or bounded form was not tried).
The cached answers are correct about the code (the truth is the same extractor's facts).
Removed tests defeat file-level caching (in the audit's hand-built case the removed test's own file was in the dependency set).
The main-chain lanes, the age table or the gap table were independently verified.
All side-branch snapshots were merged into main (90 of 91 were).
problems: Deviation from the brief: questions (b) were not generated from the first snapshot graph, because the first snapshot is the repository's first commit (237 nodes, web only: no route, table, setting, migration or test node). Anchors come from all snapshots instead, each existing in at least 20 consecutive main-chain snapshots.

Only 99 of the 190 snapshots lie on main's first-parent chain; the other 91 are on side branches. All 190 form one first-parent ancestry tree, which the primary replay uses (each snapshot inherits the cache of its nearest cached first-parent ancestor); main-chain-only replays are reported as the stride lanes.

Generated questions could not be spread evenly over runtimes: other_half, migrations_touch_table and route_clients anchors are backend only, and screen_tables has no backend anchor; per-kind runtime counts are in setup.questions.
Many fresh answers are empty (change_reach 63 %, screen_tables 60 %, invariants_on_file 42 %, tests_reach 35 %); hit rates restricted to non-empty answers are reported beside the main ones.

The first pair of runs (out/run1, out/run2) used slightly older code (no empty-answer counter, no per-policy timing, no fact_pos row, no optional seed list in the completion program); it was byte-identical between its two runs, and the reported pair (out/final1, out/final2) was re-run with the final code and is byte-identical too.
Replay timings were taken with two replays running at once on the same machine; the dependency-index bench was run alone, at one commit only.
Fact hashes are 32-bit FNV-1a; a collision would hide a change. The chance per changed fact is about 2.3e-10; it was not otherwise guarded.
Token prices per kind come from 3 to 4 held-out questions each; the completion kind has no measured derivation price and is left out of the token bound.
One of the 91 off-chain snapshots (8dafcecc7f, 342 logged lookups) is on a branch that was never merged; the first version of the notes said all were merged.
The first version of the notes called the token figure an upper bound; it uses median prices and is an estimate (AUDIT.md section 7).
The first version did not report that 55.2 % of the questions of kinds 1-8 never change; rates on the changing questions are now given.
Two rates were rounded twice in the first version (fact_pos 88.6 % for 88.548 %, completion cutoff 24.4 % for 24.45 %).
